item.title: Stacking Stars: Minimum-Area Packing with and without Rotation
item.description: arXiv:2611.07100v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the problem of packing a given set of polygons into a minimum-area convex container, that is, placing them without overlap so as to minimize the area of their convex hull. Every previously known polynomial-time algorithm with a nontrivial approximation guarantee for packing polygons with arbitrary edge orientations required the polygons to be convex. In fact, an algorithm was not even known when every input polygon was a quadrilateral. We obtain such algorithms for the entire class of star-shaped polygons with unrestricted combinatorial complexity. The stars may be just translated or also rotated. In either case, we give an $O(\log n)$-approximation algorithm, where $n$ is the number of stars. Likewise, we get $O(\log n)$-approximation algorithms for bin and strip packing, assuming that the diameter of the stars is at most some (small) constant. Previous approximation algorithms for polygon packing focused on convex objects, and the analysis always relied on a density argument, i.e., if the area of the packed objects is at least a fraction $\rho$ of the area of the container, then we have a $(1/\rho)$-approximation. However, star-shaped polygons may need an arbitrarily large area to be packed, even when the total area of the stars approaches $0$ and each star has bounded diameter. This phenomenon prevents the use of density arguments. We instead establish a strong structural property about any packing: Even though the stars can fit together in complicated ways, we can reorganize them into simple stacks, replace these stacks by rectangles, and consider a packing of these rectangles. The rearrangement costs only a factor of $O(\log n)$, which stems from the number of size groups. We complement our algorithms by showing that both the translational and the rotational versions are APX-hard, even for constant complexity stars.
item.dc:creator: Mikkel Abrahamsen, Jacobus Conradi, Arindam Khan, Jack Stade, Sampson Wong, Shuyi Yan, Hanwen Zhang

item.title: K-subareas partitioning subject to coinciding boundary segments of neighboring subareas
item.description: arXiv:2611.07701v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A method for the problem of partitioning an area into K subareas subject to coinciding boundary segments of neighboring subareas is presented. The given area may be non-convex and may additionally include obstacle areas. The proposed hierarchical method involves three steps: repeated bisection splitting, merging and the solution of traveling salesman problems. Geographic real-world outdoors areas data is used for the evaluation of the method. The benefit of computational simplicity at the cost of imbalanced subarea sizes is highlighted.
item.dc:creator: Mogens Plessen

item.title: Approximating the Euclidean Ball by Polytopes: Surprising Rates in High Dimensions
item.description: arXiv:2610.34651v2 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We provide sharp estimates on the number of vertices needed to approximate the Euclidean unit ball $B_d\subset\mathbb R^d$ with relative symmetric-difference volume error at most $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$. We show that the minimum vertex budget $N_\varepsilon(d)$ satisfies $$\log N_\varepsilon(d)\asymp d\log\left(1+\frac1{\varepsilon\sqrt d}\right).$$ In particular, $\exp(O(\sqrt d/\varepsilon))$ vertices suffice for every $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ and all sufficiently large $d$. We also prove that achieving a fixed error $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ requires at least $\Omega\bigl((\tfrac{1+\varepsilon}{2\sqrt\varepsilon})^{d-1}\bigr)$ facets, an exponential number in $d$. We extend our vertex approximation result to Gaussian symmetric-difference error, and give a positive answer to the question of De, Nadimpalli, and Servedio about subexponential vertex complexity for approximating Euclidean balls. We also disprove a Macbeath-type extremality principle for unrestricted vertex approximation. Whereas the ball uniformly maximizes the inscribed approximation error among all convex bodies (Macbeath, 1951), we show that approximating the hypercube $[-1,1]^d$ to relative error $\varepsilon$, with $\delta:=1-\varepsilon$, requires $N\ge\frac{\delta}{2}\exp(\Omega(\delta^2d/\log^2(2/\delta)))$ vertices whenever $d\ge16\log(2/\delta)$. Thus, when $d$ is large, the cube is harder to approximate than the ball in this sense. Finally, we determine the sharp dimensional order of the classical Laguerre-Delone triangulation number, showing that $\mathrm{ldel}_{d-1}=\Theta(d^{-1/2})$ as $d\to\infty$. This improves both the upper bound of Ludwig, Sch\"utt, and Werner and the lower bound of B\"or\"oczky by a factor of order $\sqrt d$. By classical asymptotic approximation theorems (Ludwig, 1999), this improvement applies to every convex body in $\mathbb R^d$ with $C^2$ boundary and positive Gaussian curvature.
item.dc:creator: Yegor Gorodzha, Steven Hoehner, Gil Kur

item.title: Resolving Tusn\'ady's Problem
item.description: arXiv:2611.06998v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We prove a lower bound of $\Omega_d((\log N)^{d-1/2})$ for the worst-case combinatorial discrepancy of $N$-point sets with respect to anchored boxes in every fixed dimension $d\ge3$. Together with Nikolov's upper bound of the same order and Wei's planar lower bound, this settles Tusn\'ady's problem: the discrepancy of axis-parallel boxes is $\Theta_d((\log N)^{d-1/2})$ in every fixed dimension $d\ge2$. The proof combines smoothed product test functions, sampling discretization, and an entropy argument for conditioned Gaussian vectors.
item.dc:creator: Nicola Wengiel

item.title: On the complexity of the free space of a translating box in R^3
item.description: arXiv:2510.22386v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Consider a convex polyhedral robot $B$ that can translate (without rotating) amidst a finite set of non-moving polyhedral obstacles in $\mathbb R^3$. The "free space" $\mathcal F$ of $B$ is the set of all positions in which $B$ is disjoint from the interior of every obstacle. Aronov and Sharir (1997) derived an upper bound of $O(n^2\log n)$ for the combinatorial complexity (number of vertices, edges, and faces) of $\mathcal F$, where $n$ is the total complexity of the obstacles, and the complexity of $B$ is assumed constant. Halperin and Yap (1993) showed that, if $B$ is either a box or a "flat" convex polygon, then a tighter bound of $O(n^2\alpha(n))$ holds. Here $\alpha(n)$ is the inverse Ackermann function. In this paper we prove that if $B$ is a box, then the complexity of $\mathcal F$ is $O(n^2)$. Furthermore, if $B$ is a convex polygon whose edges come in parallel pairs, then the complexity of $\mathcal F$ is $O(n^2)$ as well. These results settle the question of the asymptotical worst-case complexity of $\mathcal F$ for a box, as well as for all convex polygons.
item.dc:creator: Gabriel Nivasch

item.title: Two-colour crossing minimization in complete geometric graphs is NP-hard
item.description: arXiv:2610.31719v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Given a fixed straight-line drawing of a complete graph, we seek a two-colouring of its edges that minimizes monochromatic crossing pairs. We prove that the threshold decision problem is NP-complete, even for points in general position with integer coordinates. Thus exact minimization is NP-hard, resolving the complexity question posed at the Crossing Number Workshop in 2019. We reduce from MaxCut on permutation graphs by representing source vertices with classes of geometric edges, whose crossings encode source adjacencies. The target complete graph also contains every other edge between its points, and their freely chosen colours can affect the encoded cost. To control these interactions, we construct a large comparison grid with two stable colour phases and use program points to turn this reference into colour preferences on other edges. The optimum differs from a computable baseline plus the amplified minimum number of uncut source edges by an error small enough to distinguish consecutive source values. The reduction is deterministic, with polynomially many points and polynomial coordinate bit length.
item.dc:creator: Zhe Zhang, Yi Liu, Dan Yang
